    <Aside type="tip" icon="starlight" title="Reading Reflection">

    ####  Music Mouse Explained | Laurie Spiegel on Algorithmic Composition

    ##### Summary

    In this interview, Laurie Spiegel introduces Music Mouse, a software instrument designed to turn the Macintosh into something you can actually perform music with instead of just editing or sequencing sounds. The program uses algorithms to handle harmony in real time while the user controls melodic movement through spatial gestures with a mouse or trackball. Her goal is to make music creation more accessible by lowering technical barriers while still allowing expressive improvisation. Spiegel also highlights how innovation in music technology isn’t just about new sounds, but about designing new interaction methods that change how people relate to making music.

    ##### Quote

    “Unlike the majority of music software available out there, this is not an editor in any way. This is actually a program which turns the Macintosh into an instrument which you play.”

    ##### Comment

    What stood out to me is how forward-thinking Spiegel’s approach is, especially around interaction design and accessibility. She shifts the focus away from technical skill and toward expression and creativity, which feels very aligned with modern HCI ideas. Instead of requiring deep musical training, the software helps guide the user while still leaving room for personal control. In many ways, Music Mouse feels like an early version of today’s generative music tools or AI-assisted creative platforms, where the system supports the creative process without fully taking over.

    ##### Discussion Question

    How much should software help create music before it starts taking away from the artist’s creativity and control?

    ##### Related Work

    A good comparison is tools like <a href="https://www.ableton.com/en/live/">Ableton Live</a>, Tone.js, or modern AI music generators. Like Music Mouse, these platforms focus more on live experimentation and interaction instead of pre-planning everything ahead of time. Ableton, for example, lets you trigger and manipulate sounds in real time, which makes music creation feel more like performance. Similarly, generative music tools build musical logic directly into the system, supporting creativity while still giving the user control, which reflects Spiegel’s idea of creating “intelligent instruments.”

    </Aside>

    <Aside title="Project">
        <a href="https://makoninio.github.io/Born-Sinner/"><h1>Visit Project</h1></a>
        <br></br>
        <p>The project was inspired by Michelle Pera-McGhee's <a href="https://pudding.cool/2023/06/groove/">WONKY</a> digital story of QuestLove's experience producing a beat. This digital story book
        creates an interactive audio and visual experience for the user that struck a chord in a non-technical music lover like myself. From a very young age I have always loved rap especially the process of producing
        a beat. From the sampling through to adding the drum through to the mixing of the vocals, I appreciate all these parts of the craft. Given this, I love it when artists walk their fans through the production process
        as it adds a deeper level of intimacy to the listening experience. Given this, I took to my favorite rapper "J Cole" and sort to retell the story of how he produced the beat for one of his biggest records "Power Trip". Using 
        HTML, CSS and Javascript using Tone.js in particular for the interactive beat making component.</p>
